result: Serial femtosecond X-ray crystallography (SFX) data were collected at SACLA at 1 ps and 10 ps after photoexcitation, yielding dark and light-activated structures at 2.07 Å and 2.21 Å resolution, respectively.
evaluation: Claims C2, C12-C14, C106, C116-C120 collectively document the experimental setup, data collection parameters, resolution, and data deposition. The crystallographic statistics (Table 1) and methods description provide comprehensive validation of the data quality and experimental conditions.

result: Difference electron density maps at 1 ps show significant structural changes clustered around the chromophore, with the strongest signal at the pyrrole water (-8.2σ to -9.4σ). At 10 ps, similar features persist but at lower intensity, attributed to lower photoactivation yield. Fluence-dependent experiments confirm single-photon excitation.
evaluation: Claims C15-C18, C48, C109-C111 are well-supported by quantitative difference electron density data (Table 2, Figure 2) and fluence-dependent controls. The interpretation that lower 10 ps signal reflects population decay is reasonable given the time-resolved nature of the experiment.

result: The D-ring of the chromophore twists counter-clockwise by tens of degrees (modeled as 60° in monomer A, 90° in monomer B) at 1 ps, though the precision is estimated at ±25°. This twist is strongly supported by correlated negative and positive difference density features.
evaluation: Claims C3, C19, C21-C22, C59-C62 are supported by difference electron density maps (Figure 3) showing characteristic positive peaks (V, VI) indicating new positions of D-ring substituents. The authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty (±25°) and test alternative models. The counter-clockwise direction contradicts prior predictions for bacterial phytochromes but is well-supported by the data.

result: The C-ring translates by ~0.69 Å and its propionate chain detaches from conserved anchoring residues Ser272 and Ser274, accompanied by rearrangement of the water network connecting the D-ring, C-ring propionate, and His290.
evaluation: Claims C22-C23, C26-C27, C45 are supported by correlated difference density features (VII-X in Figure 3a) and the refined structural model. The mechanistic interpretation linking D-ring twist to C-ring propionate detachment is reasonable given the spatial proximity and observed structural changes.

result: The conserved His260 retracts and Tyr263 moves upward at 1 ps. A conserved helix (Ser257-Val269, >50% conserved) moves away from the chromophore by 0.36-0.62 Å, transducing D-ring changes to break the Ser257-B-ring propionate hydrogen bond.
evaluation: Claims C24-C25, C31-C34 are supported by difference density features (XI-XIV, Figure 3b) and quantitative distance measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). The conservation analysis strengthens the functional interpretation. The proposed signal transduction pathway is a reasonable inference from the structural data.

result: The B-ring propionate salt bridge to Arg254 breaks at 1 ps, not through direct B-ring movement but via disruption of a water bridge between B- and C-ring propionates and protein relaxation.
evaluation: Claims C28-C30, C35, C46 are supported by difference density on waters (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and the absence of significant B-ring changes. The mechanistic interpretation that protein relaxation is required is reasonable given the indirect nature of the observed changes.

result: The conserved pyrrole water photodissociates from the chromophore at 1 ps, an unexpected finding given its ubiquitous presence in phytochrome structures. Fluence-dependent data confirm this is not a multi-photon artifact.
evaluation: Claims C4, C36-C37, C47, C76-C79 are strongly supported by the most intense negative difference density feature (-8.2σ to -9.4σ, Table 2) and fluence-dependent controls (Figure 2) showing this signal persists at lowest excitation levels. The finding contradicts prior expectations, making it particularly significant.

result: The A-ring and Asp207 move downward at 1 ps, accompanied by backbone movements of the conserved Pro201-His209 stretch (0.54-0.57 Å away from chromophore center) and rearrangements of waters and Tyr176.
evaluation: Claims C36-C37, C39-C43, C47 are supported by difference density features (XVIII-XXIII, Figure 4) and quantitative measurements. The excellent agreement between calculated and observed difference maps (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) validates the structural interpretation. Claim C39 appropriately presents alternative interpretations for pyrrole water position.

result: The structural changes at 1 ps represent a highly collective, coordinated photoresponse involving chromophore liberation from the protein scaffold and directed backbone/water movements that channel signals toward the PHY domain.
evaluation: Claims C5, C44, C49, C89, C92, C97, C101 synthesize the individual structural observations into an integrated mechanistic picture. The interpretation is well-supported by the extensive, correlated structural changes observed throughout the binding pocket and their occurrence in conserved regions.

result: Asp207 displacement and A-ring/pyrrole water changes suggest disruption of the GAF-PHY interface may occur as early as 1 ps. When mapped onto the full photosensory core, Tyr263 (moving up) and Asp207 (moving down) work together to destabilize the Arg466:Asp207 salt bridge.
evaluation: Claims C85-C88, C90-C91 connect the observed 1 ps structural changes to known signaling mechanisms. The mapping onto the full-length structure (Figure 5b, PDB 4O0P) provides structural context. While speculative regarding the PHY-tongue (C88), the inference is reasonable given Asp207's established role and the observed movements.

result: The D-ring may rotate counter-clockwise in bacterial phytochromes (similar to plant/cyanobacterial phytochromes), requiring C-ring displacement. However, construct truncation or crystal packing effects cannot be fully excluded.
evaluation: Claims C63-C68 present speculation about the generality of the counter-clockwise rotation and potential artifacts. While the data support counter-clockwise rotation in this system (C59-C62), the authors appropriately acknowledge limitations (C66) and cite conformational heterogeneity in solution (C67). This requires validation in full-length protein and other phytochromes.

result: Pyrrole water photodissociation requires significant energy to break multiple hydrogen bonds and may be triggered by excited-state charge redistribution (e.g., proton/electron transfer) rather than direct steric interactions with the D-ring.
evaluation: Claims C80-C83 present mechanistic speculation about pyrrole water photodissociation. While C80-C81 are reasonable inferences from structural data, C82-C83 are explicitly speculative and require further investigation (as acknowledged). The proposed mechanism lacks direct experimental support in this study.

result: Comparison with Pr-to-Pfr transition shows that Tyr176 and Phe203 exhibit smaller movements at 1 ps, indicating tight coupling to the chromophore. Propionate bond breaking, required for chromophore sliding in the full transition, is part of the primary photoresponse.
evaluation: Claims C69-C75 compare the 1 ps structure to known Pr/Pfr structures. The observations (C70-C71) are supported by difference density (Table 2), and the interpretations (C72, C75) are reasonable. This contextualizes the ultrafast changes within the larger photoconversion pathway.

result: The ultrafast structural changes in phytochrome are more extensive than in other photoreceptors (bacteriorhodopsin, photoactive yellow protein, fluorescent protein) and more directed than 'protein quakes' observed in myoglobin and bacteriorhodopsin.
evaluation: Claims C94-C96 compare the phytochrome photoresponse to other systems with appropriate citations. The characterization as 'more directed' is supported by the coordinated movements in conserved regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) rather than random thermal fluctuations.

result: The multidimensional, collective photoresponse is functionally reasonable given that phytochromes must support bidirectional photoisomerization from structurally and electronically distinct Pr and Pfr states. This is consistent with characteristic low quantum yields.
evaluation: Claims C98-C100, C102-C103 provide functional context for the observed structural complexity. The reasoning is logical: bidirectional photoswitching requires different reaction trajectories (C99), and the observed complexity (C101-C102) explains low quantum yields (C103, with citation). This is interpretive but well-reasoned.

result: The D-ring twist confirms the long-standing working model for phytochrome activation, while pyrrole water photodissociation is a novel finding. Both events are proposed to work together to enable light signal transduction.
evaluation: Claims C104-C105 summarize the main findings and their significance. C104 is supported by the data confirming D-ring twist and the novelty of pyrrole water photodissociation. C105 is a reasonable synthesis, though the functional proposal requires further validation.

result: The 1 ps structure likely represents an intermediate en route to the Lumi-R state, though crystallography cannot determine electronic state. Structural information for Lumi-R is currently missing, and its low quantum yield (~10%) makes spectroscopic investigation difficult.
evaluation: Claims C51-C54 appropriately contextualize the findings within the phytochrome photocycle. The limitations of crystallography (C53) and the inference about the intermediate nature (C54) are reasonable. This provides important context for interpreting the results.

result: The average photon fluence per chromophore is estimated at 0.5-1 photons, accounting for light scattering in the grease matrix. Refinement at 1 ps used 8% photoexcitation; 10 ps refinement was aborted due to lower yield. Monomer A provided clearer difference maps despite lower signal.
evaluation: Claims C108, C113-C115 describe technical aspects of data analysis. The photon fluence estimate (C108) accounts for scattering (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and is consistent with the 8% refinement occupancy (C113). The decision to abort 10 ps refinement (C114) is justified by data quality concerns.

result: Background on phytochrome function and structure: Phytochromes control growth/reproduction/photosynthesis, exist in Pr/Pfr states providing two-color vision, contain a bilin chromophore anchored by propionates, and feature a PHY-tongue that changes secondary structure between states.
evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C11 provide established background knowledge supported by citations. These contextual claims are well-established in the field and appropriately referenced.

result: Prior knowledge: The D-ring isomerizes from Z (Pr) to E (Pfr) around C15-C16, is already isomerized in Lumi-R, and was predicted to rotate clockwise in bacterial phytochromes. Most point mutations alter but don't inhibit photoconversion.
evaluation: Claims C55, C57-C58, C93 summarize relevant prior work with appropriate citations. These provide context for interpreting the current findings, particularly the unexpected counter-clockwise rotation.

result: Conformational changes of the A-ring, Asp207, and pyrrole water on picosecond timescales had not been previously considered.
evaluation: Claim C84 establishes the novelty of the A-ring/Asp207/pyrrole water findings. This is a reasonable statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

result: The refined dark structure is very similar to a previous SFX structure (5K5B, RMSD 0.646-0.610 Å), validating data quality and reproducibility.
evaluation: Claim C112 provides validation through comparison with prior work. The low RMSD values indicate good reproducibility and data quality.
